settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: ParserConfig.getDeserializer performs a deny-prefix check that throws JSONException for denied prefixes, and deployments can extend the list via configuration/system property (seen in the read ParserConfig spans).
Feature.DisableSpecialKeyDetect can suppress special-key processing entirely.
If TypeUtils.loadClass returns null the type name may be merely stored and parsing may continue instead of instantiating.
Some downstream paths only cast or type-check the loaded class (e.g., assignability/expected-class comparisons) rather than reflectively instantiating it.
No test or runtime execution was performed; reachability from real HTTP/framework entry points was not traced in this repository.
candidates.description: DefaultJSONParser.parseObject recognizes the JSON key equal to JSON.DEFAULT_TYPE_KEY ("@type", unless DisableSpecialKeyDetect is set) and reads the following string value, calling TypeUtils.loadClass(typeName, config.getDefaultClassLoader()) with the attacker-controlled name. On success it computes a deserializer and can instantiate the class (via JavaBeanDeserializer.createInstance or clazz.newInstance()) and/or continue deserializing into the loaded type. Resolution in TypeUtils.loadClass (read region 960-1075) uses the provided class loader and falls back to context class loader / Class.forName without an allow-list. The only filtering visible in the read ParserConfig spans is a deny-prefix list checked when obtaining a deserializer, and the read default content is limited (e.g., java.lang.Thread) plus optional entries from configuration. This means many classpath classes are not blocked and the special key is processed by default. MiscCodec (read region 40-300) also treats the special-key name and, for Class-typed targets, resolves a class from JSON string input. This is a candidate, not a confirmed exploit: actual impact depends on the application classpath, the deployed ParserConfig deny list, and reachability from untrusted input, none of which were exercised.
missing_evidence: No runtime confirmation that a specific gadget class loads and has security-relevant side effects under this build.
No evidence of how downstream applications configure the ParserConfig deny list in practice.
No proof of an external input boundary mapping untrusted HTTP/body data into these parse entry points in this repository.
No verification of the JDK version / available gadget libraries in the intended deployment.
preconditions: JSON is parsed via the default parser path (e.g., JSON.parse/parseObject) without Feature.DisableSpecialKeyDetect, which is the default.
The application classpath contains an attacker-choosable class whose instantiation/deserialization side effects are security-relevant.
The effective ParserConfig deny list has not been extended to cover the relevant classes.
candidates.title: Special-key "@type" handling in DefaultJSONParser loads attacker-named classes via TypeUtils.loadClass, gated only by ParserConfig deny-prefix list
